item.title: Cardinals’ biggest mistake at 2026 NFL Trade Deadline
item.description: Cardinals’ biggest mistake at 2026 NFL Trade Deadline appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Arizona Cardinals had already signaled that they were prepared to turn the page on their struggling 2026 campaign. Trading Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jacoby Brissett showed that general manager Monti Ossenfort was willing to sacrifice established talent for future draft capital. Yet, when the trade deadline arrived, Arizona suddenly became reluctant to part with two of its most valuable veterans. This left the Cardinals with a missed opportunity to accelerate their rebuild. For a team sitting near the bottom of the NFC West, holding onto valuable assets could prove more costly than letting them go. Bottom-dweller Joe Camporeale-Imagn Images Sitting at 3-6 and anchored to the bottom of the NFC West, Arizona’s 2026 campaign has unraveled under first-year head coach Mike LaFleur. The Cardinals opened with an encouraging road victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, but three consecutive defeats quickly exposed their defensive vulnerabilities. They later bounced back with hard-fought wins over the Rams and Dallas Cowboys, only to lose to Denver and Seattle. Arizona’s defense has surrendered 28.3 points per game. Injuries have devastated the offense. Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr., running back Jeremiyah Love, wide receiver Michael Wilson, and quarterback Gardner Minshew II have all landed on Injured Reserve. With Carson Beck now taking over at quarterback , the franchise has little reason to prioritize short-term results over long-term roster construction . Failing to cash in That reality makes Ossenfort’s inaction on deadline day particularly puzzling. Arizona had already demonstrated a willingness to accumulate draft capital. Trading Harrison to Houston for a 2027 second-round pick and a seventh-round selection, while sending a 2027 sixth-rounder to the Texans. The Cardinals also dealt Brissett to Baltimore for a 2027 fourth-rounder and a 2028 seventh-round pick. And yet, Baker and Sweat remained in Arizona after the November 10 deadline. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Baker was arguably the biggest missed opportunity. The Buffalo Bills reportedly made a compelling offer for the veteran safety. Arizona ultimately held firm. Buffalo pivoted to Tennessee’s Amani Hooker. They acquired him for a second-round pick while receiving a fifth-rounder in return. Reports indicated that the Cardinals viewed Baker as the emotional heartbeat of the franchise and were reluctant to move him. There is certainly a human element to that decision. Baker has been a franchise icon and one of the most recognizable faces of the organization. At the same time, sentimentality cannot become a substitute for sound roster management. item.title: Sean O’Malley Has Idea for Usman Nurmagomedov’s UFC Debut
item.description: Sean O'Malley Usman Nurmagomedov UFC Getty Former UFC bantamweight champion Sean O’Malley has an idea for Usman Nurmagomedov’s UFC debut whenever he signs with the promotion. Despite being sentenced to six months in prison for his role in a gang attack against Merab Dvalishvili at an Abu Dhabi hotel earlier this week, the UFC is still expected to sign Nurmagomedov once he gets out of prison. When that happens, O’Malley knows just the fight for him. Sean O’Malley Suggests Usman Nurmagomedov Fights Ilia Topuria Speaking on his YouTube channel, O’Malley suggested that Nurmagomedov fights former UFC lightweight champion Ilia Topuria for his debut. “Does this set up a fight between Ilia Topuria and Usman Nurmagomedov? That’s a crazy fight. That’s a crazy, hard fight for Ilia to bounce back from. It’s an insane fight for Usman to jump into the UFC pool. It is a fight that I want to see. I mean, Ilia vs. Paddy (Pimblett) is up there, Ilia vs. Usman is up there. These are huge, massive, insane numbered main events that don’t have any titles on the line. … I think Usman vs. Ilia makes sense. That’s the fight to make. That would be a crazy fight. Ilia’s big, but he’s not tall. He’s 5-6, Usman’s probably 6-1. it would be a tough fight for both guys. It would be an interesting fight. The storyline’s there,” O’Malley said (via MMAjunkie.com ). Will the UFC Book This Fight? The idea of a Nurmagomedov vs. Topuria fight is certainly one that makes a lot of sense given that both men have a lot of bad blood against one another, especially in the wake of the attack on Dvalishvili, who is a close friend of Topuria’s. That being said, it seems far more likely that Topuria will fight Paddy Pimblett next, as that’s the fight that has been teased for several months now, and one that makes more sense based on the UFC rankings. But we all know the UFC is a business, so don’t be surprised if and when the UFC inks Nurmagomedov to a contract, that he gets a huge name in his debut with the promotion. This article was originally published on HEAVY The post Sean O’Malley Has Idea for Usman Nurmagomedov’s UFC Debut appeared first on HEAVY .

item.title: Xavier 81-63 Mississippi State: Recap
item.description: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 23: Tru Washington #3 of the Xavier Musketeers brings the ball up court against the Kent State Golden Flashes during the second half of an exhibition game at Cintas Center on October 23, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Tanner Pearson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Winning all the buy games in the world by 45 is nice, but it isn’t going to move the needle in March when it comes time to evaluate a team’s resume for the NCAA Tournament. To get there, you have to beat someone with substance at some point and Xavier took their first chance to do so with style tonight at The Greenbrier. Mississippi State is not expected to challenge at the top of the SEC this season, but they are a solid Q2 opportunity on a neutral floor and the first line on a resume Xavier hopes to fill out before Selection Sunday. The Bulldogs grabbed the first four points of the night, but Xavier punched back immediately and never gave the lead back after Tru Washington (21/8/4) put on a personal 5-0 run. Washington was Xavier’s star tonight, but he was far from alone in putting his stamp on the first half as Nikos Chitikoudis (11/6/1) stepped into the void left by Mike Nwoko’s (4/6/1) foul issues and gave Xavier 12 excellent minutes in the first frame. Xavier started to gain separation near the midway point of the half when Ruben Dominguez (9/0/0) was fouled shooting a three and cashed out all three free throws then cut out the middle man and drained a three the next time down to put X up 7 and put the Bulldogs on the ropes. Mississippi State star Josh Hubbard sparked to life to bring the game back to within a point with 3:34 to play, but Xavier grabbed back the momentum through back to back threes from Kalek House (3/4/3) and Gabriel Pozzato (9/1/0) and, after a bit of back and forth, a four point play from Pozzato stake Xavier to a 10 point halftime lead and gave this team a chance to show they had learned from last year’s heartbreaks and could close out a contest. In a series of events familiar to people who remembered the first half of the game, Mississippi State scored first and then Tru Washington scored Xavier’s first five points followed by a Nikos Chitikoudis bucket. That pushed the lead to a dozen and a triple from Jovan Milicevic (12/3/0) prompted a Chris Jans timeout and put Xavier in a spot where they were well and truly in the driver’s seat. The test from there was one of game management. Mississippi State cranked up the pressure and tried to make Xavier guard someone other than Hubbard, who was hounded off the litany of ball screens the Bulldogs ran for him all night. The only time it really threatened to get interesting was when Mississippi State cut the lead back to 12 with 14:26 to play, but Xavier responded with a quick 6-0 run to put the Bulldogs back on the mat and it was never closer than 14 after that point. item.title: Bloom-Carroll volleyball title hopes fall short in state semifinal
item.description: VANDALIA — During its tournament run to the state volleyball tournament, the Bloom-Carroll volleyball team was always able to overcome some early pitfalls, and during their Division III state semifinal against Padua Franciscan, it looked as if the Bulldogs were going to follow the same script. The Bears won the first set, but Bloom-Carroll came right back to tie it up in the second. In the all-important third set, the Bulldogs could not get over the hump and lost a heartbreaker. The Bulldogs were not able to overcome that, and the Bears were able to finish them off in the fourth set and post a 25-22, 22-25, 28-26, 25-14 victory on Friday night, Nov. 13, at Vandalia-Butler High School. More: 'We want to win it all' | Bloom Carroll eyes state title Even though the Bulldogs fought back, they made some uncharacteristic mistakes, and in the end, it cost them. “We struggled, especially in that fourth set, and I think it’s one of those things where you really don’t want to think it could come to an end,” Bloom-Carroll coach Kyle McFerin said. “I thought we made winning plays in the third set, and we played to win, but we couldn’t get the win, and then we came out flat in the fourth set. We just couldn’t get it going. We kind of got in our own way at times, with more net calls than we usually get, and we hit a few more balls out-of-bounds than we usually do. This is a state semifinal game, and you can’t do those things and expect to win.” The third set was crucial and could have gone either way. Each time the Bulldogs were forced to score, they did, but they could never take the lead down the stretch and eventually fell. “We were right there in the fourth set, but they were able to make a few more plays,” McFerin said. “If we win that, who knows how things would have turned out.” Alya Mitchell had a solid game and led the Bulldogs with 15 kills. Renee Smith had 30 assists, and Kylynne Solberger had 19 digs. Josie Burr chipped in eight kills, Kylee Reiser finished with five kills, 10 digs and five aces, and Maddie Fox added seven kills. Bloom-Carroll, which went undefeated in the Mid-State League-Buckeye Division, finishes with a 22-5 overall record. The Bulldogs were state runner-up in 2025 and made back-to-back state tournament appearances for the first time in school history. Over the last two years, they have won 49 games. Bloom-Carroll’s five seniors have helped raise the bar for the program. “It is hard right now, but the five seniors we had were great this year,” McFerin said. “This was a challenging season in a lot of ways, but they responded, and we grew together. We weren't a team at the beginning of the season, and we became a team as the season went on, and that’s hard to do. They did a great job of progressing, and that’s a credit to them. They have been to two straight final fours, and they have done a great job moving the program forward.” Tom Wilson is a sports reporter for the Lancaster Eagle-Gazette. item.title: Lafayette Jeff football's postseason ends in regional with loss to Warsaw
item.description: LAFAYETTE — Jeff football lined up together on its side of the field, as it does every week, but it wasn’t in the same way its grown accustomed to over the last several weeks. The Bronchos made history with their third consecutive sectional championship this season, but the road ended at the regional once again with a 49-39 loss to Warsaw on Friday, Nov. 13. On the other side of the field, the Tigers celebrated their second regional title with the trophy raised in the air. Coach Pat Shanley acknowledged it was one that hurt. He called senior leader Ka’vion Campbell-Walker up to make a departing speech, who commanded every player’s attention with a passionate message to the underclassmen to carry on the work when he’s gone. More: Lafayette area IHSAA football regional championship game scores, updates More: Benton Central's Claire Whaley voted Nov. 2-8 J&C Athlete of the Week, sponsored by Ivy Tech He and other seniors, such as wide receiver Bryce VanOstran, quarterback Trysten Barrett and defensive lineman Chris Hardy, have laid the foundation for the program over the years. That group has helped them get to a place where they can be surefire sectional winners each season and have chances to make it deeper into November. The Bronchos couldn’t quite kick down the doors of regional this year. But they have no doubts that they’ll continue to build the foundation up and accomplish that soon. “We have a program that is only going to continue to get better,” Shanley said. “We have people in this community that are really committed and understand what we’re doing and what we’re building. You have kids that really believe in it and they love it. … We’re going to fight, claw and scratch to find ways to get better and to kick that door in. “It’s just a matter of time.” On the opening drive, VanOstran got the crowd at Schuemann Stadium fired up with a 63-yard touchdown at the 10:01 mark of the first quarter off a pass from Barrett. It was a whole lot of yards after the catch, and VanOstran skipped his way to celebrate the moment in front of the crowd. That was the energy Jeff needed to start the night. But Warsaw’s flexbone triple option offense, a style of play that Jeff has grown to be familiar with over the years, quickly took over. The Tigers tied it up at 7-7 at the 5:11 mark, but their next drive signaled something that the Broncho defense couldn’t contain for the rest of the game. Quarterback Mark Haynes broke loose and went untouched for an 80-yard touchdown with 1:27 remaining in the first, before converting a two-point conversion to give Warsaw a 15-10 lead. The defensive breakdowns happened again at the 3:22 mark in the second, in which Brady Sauer bounced to the outside and down the sideline for a 50-yard touchdown on fourth-and-2. By the end of the first half, the Tigers led 29-10. “You got to stop a quarterback/fullback, right? item.title: Blazers’ Robert Williams III puts Dylan Cardwell on a poster during Kings clash
item.description: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images Blazers’ Robert Williams III puts Dylan Cardwell on a poster during Kings clash appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Portland Trail Blazers are flying high after sweeping the Oklahoma City Thunder in back-to-back games at home. Those wins put the Blazers up to 8-3, fifth in the very competitive Western Conference. The Blazers are searching for their third straight win on Friday against the Sacramento Kings in the NBA Cup. Robert Williams III is doing his part with a thunderous lob dunk, putting Dylan Cardwell on a poster . Robert Williams III RISES over his defender for the poster slam 😤 pic.twitter.com/e787bMdNnu Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPoints) November 14, 2026 After setting the screen for Jrue Holiday, Time Lord rolled hard to the rim and emphatically finished the perfectly executed lob from his teammate. Williams, who was part of the blockbuster trade that sent Holiday to the Boston Celtics back in 2023 , has had an injury-hit time in Portland. He played just 85 games over his first three seasons with the team, 59 of which came last season. But he’s been more present for the Blazers this season, appearing in nine of the team’s 11 games prior to their clash with the Kings. He’s averaging 7.6 points and 6.6 rebounds in 16.4 minutes per game as Donovan Clingan’s backup off the Blazers bench. With Clingan and Williams, the Blazers have one of the more imposing defensive center combinations in the league. When healthy and at his best, Williams is a supremely athletic rim protector who can sky up for some highlight-reel slams from time to time. If he stays healthy, he figures to play an important role in the Blazers’ rotation moving forward. That’s a big “if” given his checkered injury history, but for now, the Blazers are glad he is healthy and playing. item.title: Enugu community in leadership crisis over disputed constitution, PG election
item.description: …Group alleges 22-year concealment of registered constitution ..Dispute over rotational principle, five-year tenure of Ikenge . ..Cabinet scribe distances self, blames PG’s kinsmen By Steve Oko A leadership crisis has erupted in Eziowa, Aguobu Owa Autonomous Community, Ezeagu Central Local Government Area of Enugu State, over the interpretation of the community’s constitution and the emergence of a new President-General of its Town Union. The crisis centres on allegations by a group, Concerned People of Eziowa, that a part of the community’s constitution, registered on February 8, 2004, was kept away from the people for about 22 years, resulting in disagreements over leadership succession and the tenure of traditional and town union office holders. The group, in a statement signed by Ozo Dr Ejike Orji on its behalf, alleged that a Certified True Copy (CTC) of the constitution initially made available to the community did not contain Page 23, which it said contains provisions governing the tenure and selection of members of the Igwe’s Cabinet and the office of Ikenge. It said a subsequent search at the Enugu State Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs enabled it to obtain another certified copy containing the disputed page. According to the group, the provisions of Page 23 stipulate a five-year review of the tenure of members of the Igwe’s Cabinet and provide for rotational occupation of the office of Ikenge among the community’s three villages, excluding the village that produces the reigning traditional ruler. It alleged that the office of Ikenge had remained with one individual beyond the stipulated period, arguing that the position was due for rotation between Ezema and Umudim villages. The group also cited Article Seven (1) of Page 12 of the constitution, which it said provides for a four-year tenure for the President-General and other Town Union executive members. It maintained that, following the expiration of the tenure of the previous executive in 2024, the process of electing a successor commenced in line with the constitutional provisions. According to the statement, Ezema Village, which it claimed was next in line to produce the President-General, constituted an electoral committee that conducted elections into the positions allocated to the village and announced the winners. However, the group alleged that disagreement arose after some stakeholders accepted the outcome of the village electoral committee in respect of other positions but rejected its choice of candidate for the office of President-General. It claimed that some stakeholders were insisting on a different candidate and had approached the state ministry over recognition of their preferred choice. The group, however, maintained that its preferred candidate emerged through the process prescribed by the community’s constitution. item.title: PRIVATE JETS: Calls grow for tougher sanctions against erring operators
item.description: By Dickson Omobola Experts in the aviation sector have called for stricter oversight of private and charter aircraft operators in the country and urged relevant agencies to strengthen flight surveillance, improve information-sharing and impose stiffer sanctions on operators found violating aviation regulations. The experts raised concerns over regulatory enforcement following two recent serious incidents involving private aircraft: a private jet, registration number N989BC, operated by VMO Aero Ltd, which landed on a road in the Ogwashi-Uku area of Delta State, and a Challenger 604 aircraft, registration number T7-SEI, operated by Triton Aviation, whose crew reported that a door had opened in flight They particularly questioned the handling of the Asaba incident and raised concerns about the absence of a final investigation report and the enforcement actions taken against the pilot and the company responsible for managing the aircraft. One of the experts also queried the regulatory oversight of foreign-registered private jets operating in Nigeria, alleging that some operators might be exploiting their connections to influential individuals to evade regulatory requirements. Speaking to Vanguard, General Secretary of the Aviation Safety Round Table Initiative, ART, Mr Olumide Ohunayo, expressed concern that months after the Asaba incident, the authorities had yet to provide a comprehensive account of the investigation and the actions taken. “The DSS stepped in, the Ministry of Aviation, the NCAA, even the accident investigation body, yet nobody has come to tell us what they have done. Yes, there was a preliminary report, but I think we want to know what happened to that pilot. Are they not supposed to prosecute the pilot? What about the organisation that managed that aircraft? “I don’t think we should panic (both incidents). There is no red flag as far as I am concerned. There is this distinction between private and commercial operations. Yes, worldwide, commercial operations are stricter. There are more levels and layers of safety and certification that are compulsory before you can fly, compared to private operations. I think these incidents, which are also serious incidents, are meant to strengthen the regulations and processes in place.” Also speaking, aviation security expert, Group Captain John Ojikutu, retd, questioned the enforcement of regulations governing foreign-registered private aircraft operating in the country. He said: “How many of those aircraft are Nigerian-registered? They are all foreign-registered. What is the enforcement of regulation on them? One big man will get the aircraft, and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority, NCAA, will not want to get too involved because of the big man or whoever has it, or if the person has contact with the political officeholders. “After the Asaba incident, what has been the report? item.title: US Flight Ground Stop: What we know about disruption
item.description: The United States has lifted a nationwide flight ground stop that lasted more than four hours, marking the longest shutdown of departing flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) attributed Friday’s disruption to what it described as “extraordinary circumstances” arising from a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres across the country. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the incident resulted from an attack, assuring that passengers and aviation personnel were safe throughout the disruption. Here are the major details of the incident. How many flights were affected? The ground stop resulted in more than 8,500 flight delays and nearly 8,000 cancellations on Friday, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. The FAA initially announced the restriction at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (20:54 GMT), directing that all departing flights within the United States remain grounded until further notice. More than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the order was issued. While some were diverted to alternative airports, others continued to their intended destinations. Several hours later, the FAA began allowing limited departures, including flights from San Francisco International Airport. The agency officially reopened US airspace at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (01:15 GMT on Saturday). What happened to international flights? The disruption also affected international aviation, with flights bound for the United States from countries within the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, known as Eurocontrol, suspended at the FAA’s request. Eurocontrol confirmed on its website that the suspension was due to technical problems affecting US aviation operations. The organisation has 42 member states, including European Union countries, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, Turkey, Israel and Morocco. Sydney Airport, Australia’s largest international airport, also grounded all US-bound flights pending further notice. Air Canada equally cancelled flights between the United States and Canada. When will normal flight operations resume? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that the disruption would have consequences for airline operations over several days, even after the ground stop was lifted. “It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” he said at a news conference on Friday night. Duffy disclosed that tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports across the country, with many uncertain about where they would spend the night. Major airlines announced different recovery plans following the reopening of US airspace. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations, while American Airlines said it was working to operate as many remaining flights as possible that evening. JetBlue Airways announced that it would resume flights on Saturday morning. What caused the ground stop

item.title: Ageing US air traffic equipment triggers repeated flight disruptions
item.description: The nationwide grounding of departing flights across the United States on Friday was the second such shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks, highlighting recurring problems with ageing air traffic control equipment and communications infrastructure. The latest disruption, which affected air traffic control centres across the country, is part of a series of technical failures that have repeatedly disrupted flight operations in the US over the past three years. Although Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to upgrade the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ageing air traffic control systems and recruit more controllers, the Trump administration is seeking an additional $30 billion to complete the modernisation programme. Recent incidents have exposed vulnerabilities in the country’s aviation infrastructure, with communications outages, data-link failures and automation problems causing widespread delays and cancellations. Major disruptions in recent years November 13, 2026: Nationwide ground stop The FAA grounded all departing flights across the US after air traffic control centres experienced a communications outage. According to flight-tracking service FlightAware, airlines cancelled more than 1,000 flights and delayed nearly 10,000 others. September 21, 2026: East Coast disruption The FAA suspended flights to airports in New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Washington for eight hours after the primary and backup data links at the Philadelphia regional air traffic control facility failed. The incident resulted in about 9,500 flight delays and cancellations across the country. The disruption coincided with the arrival of 130 world leaders in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. Dallas and Denver disruptions A data service outage at the FAA’s Dallas Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), which manages aircraft movements between airports and higher-altitude airspace, forced the agency to impose ground stops at two airports in the Dallas area. More than 1,800 flights were delayed, while hundreds were cancelled. The FAA subsequently said contractor L3Harris had failed to ensure that backup systems were in place. However, L3Harris told NBC 5 in Dallas that the outages were preventable and resulted from inadequate US government investment in replacing outdated analogue telecommunications circuits that had reached the end of their operational life. A day before the Dallas incident, a separate automation failure in Denver forced the FAA to slow flights into Denver International Airport, resulting in average delays of between 30 and 45 minutes. April-May 2025: Newark and Philadelphia Several telecommunications outages over a number of weeks at the FAA’s Philadelphia TRACON repeatedly disrupted flight operations at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey. item.title: US resumes flights after nationwide air traffic failure
item.description: The United States has reopened its airspace after a nationwide ground stop triggered by a communications failure at air traffic control centres disrupted thousands of flights and left tens of thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the country. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the restriction on Friday, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announcing that US airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT on Saturday). However, Duffy warned that flight operations would resume gradually, adding that airlines would need time to restore normal schedules. “It’s going to be slow,” he told reporters at the White House. According to flight-tracking platform FlightRadar24, more than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, while another 1,500 flights had already been cancelled for Sunday. Aviation analysts warned that the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline operations for several days. Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports nationwide following the disruption. He disclosed that he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump at the Oval Office to discuss the incident. What caused the disruption Duffy said the problem began at 3:36 p.m. when air traffic control centres experienced instability in their radar and communications systems. According to him, switches and routers became overloaded with data, resulting in inconsistencies in information transmitted through the network and prompting authorities to shut down the affected system. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down,” he said. He maintained that authorities never completely lost radar or communications capabilities and were able to land thousands of aircraft safely. Duffy said the immediate technical problem had been resolved and that flying was safe, but stressed the need for a comprehensive upgrade of the country’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure. FG seeks $50bn for aviation overhaul The Transportation Secretary blamed inadequate congressional funding for delays in modernising the country’s air traffic control system, calling for $50 billion to overhaul the infrastructure. Earlier on Friday, before the disruption, the White House and the Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve $30.1 billion for upgrades to the nation’s ageing airports and air traffic control infrastructure. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “Give us the money to fix it.” Meanwhile, Mullin said there was no evidence so far that the incident resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue artificial intelligence system, although investigators had not ruled out either possibility. “It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we’re still looking,” he said. item.title: Women and race to 2027
item.description: Going by the number of women that have emerged candidates in the last primary elections of all the political parties in Nigeria, next year’s general polls is bound to witness fewer number of women contesting elective positions. Weekend Trust reports that while more women indicated interests in contesting by obtaining forms to secure the tickets of their parties, most of them could not go beyond the preliminary stages, with many of them either withdrawing, not considered in the consensus arrangements, or defeated in the early stages. Checks by our correspondents revealed that a higher number of women had indicated interests in contesting for state assembly seats, but the number dwindled for those going for House of Representatives seats, again, dropping drastically for Senate and getting terribly low on governorship. When the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) released the names of the presidential candidates for 2027, only two out of the 18 candidates, which constitutes 11.1per cent of the total candidates, are women, despite making up 49.32 per cent of Nigeria’s population. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers They are up against 15 men, including President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and other candidates across the political parties. The two women are Ada Elizabeth Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP) and Esther Iken Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM). Also, there are four female vice presidential candidates who will be contesting. These are Hajiya Bintu Konto (LP), Ofordile Peace Egobia (APP), Nafisat Usaku (DLA) and Patience Key (YPP) INEC figures obtained by Weekend Trust, showed that 469 women are among the 4,863 candidates listed for the Senate and House of Representatives elections, while only two of the 18 presidential candidates are women. The figures indicate that fewer than one in every 10 candidates contesting the National Assembly elections is female, while women constitute just over one in every 10 presidential candidates. The Senate has the lowest female representation, with 123 women among 1,303 candidates, representing 9.4 per cent. The House of Representatives has 346 female candidates out of 3,560, representing 9.7 per cent. The figures were calculated from the party and gender fields contained in INEC’s final list of candidates. The figures reflect a pattern in Nigerian politics in which women participate extensively in elections but remain largely absent from the institutions where political decisions are made. Data from 2015 show that only one woman contested the presidency, while four women were listed as vice presidential candidates, with 14 political parties participating. By 2019, female participation had increased, with five women contesting the presidency and 2

item.title: US grounds all departing flights over communication failure
item.description: US aviation authorities on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights following a communication failure affecting air traffic control centres, causing disruption and confusion among travellers across the country. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the order was issued after a technical problem affected communications across all Air Route Traffic Control Centres. In a statement, the agency said its technicians were investigating the problem. “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” the agency said. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” The nationwide grounding is relatively rare, as similar restrictions in recent years have generally been limited to individual airlines and lasted a few hours or less. In January 2023, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop following an outage involving its Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which provides pilots with critical information about hazards, changes to airport facilities and other developments that could affect flight operations. The disruption lasted just under two hours and was considered at the time to be the first nationwide flight grounding since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Friday’s incident came a day after US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy formally requested $30.1 billion from Congress to upgrade and modernise the country’s air traffic control system. In a letter to lawmakers, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought described the proposed investment as essential to strengthening the nation’s aviation infrastructure. “This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure,” they wrote. The impact of the grounding was already being felt at airports, with passengers at Las Vegas airport reportedly informed by Southwest Airlines check-in staff that no flights would be taking off for 24 hours. …Canadian Affairs The post US grounds all departing flights over communication failure appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: World Diabetes Day: High cost pushes drugs, special diets out of reach
item.description: As the world marks the 2026 World Diabetes Day today, attention is once again drawn to the importance of early diagnosis, timely treatment and sustained care in preventing complications and saving lives. But for many Nigerians living with the condition, the challenge goes beyond early detection to affording medication, special diets and regular medical checks needed to manage the disease. Some patients who spoke to Weekend Trust said the rising cost of treatment had pushed them into financial hardship, forcing them to ration prescribed drugs, compromise their diets or go for days without medication. For Mrs Ngunengen Akpam, living with diabetes has become a daily struggle, not only against the disease but also against the rising cost of managing it. Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers Women and race to 2027 The burden is compounded by her responsibility to also support her diabetic mother, Mama Lydia Acka, making the cost of medication, food and routine medical care a constant source of worry for the family. Akpam told one of our correspondents that the prices of essential diabetes medications had increased considerably over the years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain the treatment prescribed by her doctors. She recalled that Metformin, one of the drugs she takes, which sold for N700 for a pack of three cards in 2015, now costs about N2,500. Similarly, Dormin, which previously sold for N700, now costs N3,500 for a pack of 10 cards, she said. “The cost of drugs has increased tremendously. I take my medication twice daily, so it is not easy. In a month, we spend so much, especially when you have another diabetic person to cater for,” she said. Medication, however, is only part of the financial burden. Akpam explained that managing diabetes also requires adherence to a carefully regulated diet, including millet, beans and vegetables, which have also become expensive. Although the price of millet had dropped from more than N1,200 to N600 per mudu during the harvest season, she said her financial circumstances still made it difficult to consistently afford the recommended food items. The experience is similar for Mrs Elahi Onu, who has lived with diabetes for 11 years and whose treatment has become a major financial responsibility for her children. Onu said her children spend at least N25,000 monthly on medication alone, while more than N60,000 goes into providing the special diet recommended for managing her condition. She listed unripe plantain, beans, vegetables, basmati rice and grains such as millet among the food items she had been advised to eat. “These special types of food are costly and drain the pockets of my children. “Sometimes there is a delay in supplies of these items to me. I will be forced to go hungry for the period or fall back to any available food,” she said. Beyond feeding and medication, Onu said she also had to contend with the cost of routine medical examinations. She disclosed that one of her prescr

item.title: Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity
item.description: As the campaign season hots up, families of the abducted children in Borno and Niger states are still looking up to the authorities for intervention. Weekend Trust reports that while the pupils kidnapped in Borno have spent 213 days in captivity, students abducted in Niger have also remained in the hands of their captors for more than two weeks. Today makes it 213 days of agony and sleepless nights for the families of the abducted children in Mussa and Lassa communities of Askira-Uba Local Government Area in Borno State. The78 children, including toddlers less than two years old, who were abducted following two separate operations by bandits and insurgents, are still in captivity, even as politicians intensify campaigns for political power. The nightmare began on May 15, 2026 when at least 42 pupils and students were taken from their classrooms in Mussa Primary and Secondary School. Weeks later, on June 29, another set of 36 students were abducted in Government Day Secondary School, Lassa, further escalating security concerns in the area. Women and race to 2027 How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market Since then, the whereabouts of the children have remained unknown, plunging the families into a state of painful trauma. The Mussa school children were abducted on the same day as the 44 pupils and teachers from a school in the Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State. But unlike the Mussa schoolchildren that have remained in captivity, the Oyo children were rescued on July 10, 2026 after 56 days in captivity after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu gave marching orders to heads of security operatives to rescue them. Weekend Trust reports that parents of the abducted pupils in Borno have on various occasions expressed frustration over what they described as “silence” from both the federal and state governments. The families are alleging that the authorities have entirely abandoned them; expressing fear that their children may have been forgotten by the same people they voted to power to protect them. The chairman of the parents of the abducted children, Mr Ishaku Suya, told our correspondent that the communities had remained in despair since the abduction of the schoolchildren. “Officially, I have not heard anything from the federal or state governments. Nobody is saying anything. And nobody has reached out to us from the side of the abductors,” he said. According to him, the mothers of the abducted children are always crying and thinking about their condition. “As men, we cannot cry, but we can’t eat food whenever we remember that our toddlers, some of them less than 2 years old, are still in the hands of their abductors. We all feel abandoned,” he said. He said that many grieving parents, who are tired of empty promises from the authorities, have resorted to constant prayers. “Recently, a delegation of mothers from Mussa arranged to travel to Maiduguri to appeal directly to the Borno State governor, Babagana Umara Zulum for immediate intervention,” h

item.title: How IDPs built Abuja’s largest beans market
item.description: Ibrahim Philemon was compelled to abandon everything he had built in his youth and flee his native Gwoza for Karu in Nasarawa State because of Boko Haram’s relentless attacks on his community. Philemon is among thousands of other farmers who fled their towns because of intensified security risks posed by Boko Haram militants. But these farmers, despite facing adversity, remained undeterred. As internally displaced persons (IDPs), they were determined to rebuild their lives after the devastation caused by Boko Haram. Today, Philemon produces over 100 bags of beans and over 50 bags of maize annually since coming to Karu in 2013 as an internally displaced person. Amidst campaigns, Borno, Niger children remain in captivity Tinubu booed at Abuja mosque after Friday prayers When Boko Haram captured Gwoza town, which had an estimated population of around 388,600 in August 2014, thousands fled immediately to many states in the country and the neighbouring towns in Cameroon. Gwoza, which is located on the fringes of Sanbisa forest, is about 135 kilometres southeast of Maiduguri, the capital of Borno State. It is marked by a hilly terrain. As farmers, the displaced persons established approximately 13 camps in Karu Local Government Area of Nasarawa State, where they commenced agricultural activities. With an estimated population of over 20,000, according to the International Organisation for Migration in Nasarawa, the IDPs spread across farming communities in Karu and Keffi, seeking farmlands and clearing bushes and forests that were hitherto uncultivated to plant beans and maize. Some of them harvested over 200 bags of beans (cowpea) and maize. Within three years of their arrival, these displaced farmers rose from the ashes to establish one of the most vibrant grain markets on the outskirts of Abuja, the country’s capital, which today attracts buyers across the country. Setting up a beans market As they continued to record good harvests, selling their produce in good value immediately became a huge challenge that devastated many of them who were trying to find life after the colossal losses inflicted on them back home in Gwoza. That challenge gave birth to the establishment of what is today known as the foremost beans market in 2016, located in Auta Balefi, along the Abuja-Keffi expressway, about 25 kilometres from the Aso Rock Villa, before the National Agricultural Showground. They told our reporter, who spent a day with them, that farming and trading provided opportunities for them to rebuild their lives after displacement. David Yakubu, the secretary of the beans market, told Weekend Trust how the idea came about. He said the market was established after they encountered difficulties selling their agricultural produce at profitable prices in Ibadan, Oyo State. item.title: Emperor, 8,000 soldiers and lesson for Nigeria
item.description: I came looking for ancient soldiers and left thinking about Nigeria’s tourism potential. One thing I was particularly looking forward to during my visit to China was seeing the famous Terracotta Warriors in Xi’an. I had read about them, seen pictures, and of course, watched films inspired by the mysteries of ancient China. But nothing quite prepared me for the experience of standing in front of thousands of life-sized soldiers who have been buried underground for more than 2,000 years. And what an experience it was! If you have watched Hollywood’s The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, you may remember the mysterious army of clay soldiers that comes alive. Well, I finally got to see the real thing. Thankfully, none of them came alive while I was there. But standing in those enormous exhibition halls, surrounded by thousands of soldiers, horses and chariots arranged in military formation, I couldn’t help wondering what must have gone through the minds of the people who created this extraordinary army. The story takes us back to 221 BC when Qin Shi Huang became the first emperor to unify China. Like many powerful rulers of his time, he was obsessed with immortality and the idea of continuing his reign beyond death. His solution was to build an entire underground army to protect him in the afterlife. Think about that. While some people prepared for retirement, this emperor was preparing for eternity, complete with his own military formation. The scale of the project is difficult to comprehend. Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, horses and chariots were painstakingly created. Above the excavation pit in Xi’an, I stood where visitors have looked down on the Terracotta Army for decades: thousands of figures, each made by hand, and still not fully unearthed. What makes the discovery even more fascinating is that the soldiers are not identical. They have different facial features, hairstyles, uniforms and expressions. They look like real individuals, each with a distinct identity and military rank. Then comes another remarkable twist. For over 2,000 years, this enormous army remained hidden beneath the earth until 1974 when some local farmers digging a well stumbled upon fragments of what would become one of the greatest archaeological discoveries in modern history. Imagine going out to dig a well and discovering an entire army. I wonder what the conversation was like that evening when they returned home. Today, the site is recognised globally as one of the greatest archaeological treasures in the world, and is popularly described as the Eighth Wonder of the World. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) designated the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor a World Heritage Site in 1987. But beyond the fascinating history, what struck me most was what China has done with this discovery. This is where the story becomes particularly interesting for Nigeria. China has not simply uncovered an ancient treasure and left it

item.title: After 6 decades, LUTH struggles for survival
item.description: The Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH), located at the Idi-Araba area of Lagos State, a full-fledged medical school and tertiary hospital, was established in July 1962. The federal medical institution was established to provide advanced medical services, train medical and other health care professionals and conduct research aimed at improving health care delivery in Nigeria At a point, LUTH was regarded the pride of Africa as people all over the continent came there to seek medical treatment. In 2022, the federal medical facility clocked 60. The then Chief Medical Director (CMD), Professor Chris Bode, had disclosed that the hospital had grown from a little above 300 beds to a 1000-bed medical facility and served over 25million patients. Bode said the hospital had pioneered small incision cataract excision surgery in Nigeria and trained over 40 doctors from all over the country in the procedure in the past years. He added that LUTH had also commenced laparoscopic general and gynaecologic surgery, which according to him, had dramatically reduced the duration of hospitalisation after surgery. “Since 1962, the Lagos University Teaching Hospital has contributed in no small way in the training of medical and paramedical personnel; and our products are found across all hospitals and health care facilities, both within and outside the shore of Nigeria. “As an institution, LUTH has grown from a 500-bedded hospital to 760-bed, and then to over 1000-bedded hospital serving over 25million Lagosians and its neighbouring states. “LUTH has pioneered small incision cataract excision surgery in Nigeria and has trained over 40 doctors from all over the country in the procedure in the past years. The hospital has also commenced laparoscopic general and gynaecologic surgery, which has dramatically reduced the duration of hospitalisation after surgery. “LUTH also boasts of a comprehensive diagnostic centre and VIP clinic, state of the art laboratories, radiodiagnosis, radiotherapy and renal dialysis facilities. From a humble beginning of 330 beds, LUTH today is the largest teaching hospital in Nigeria with over 1,000 beds. The College of Medicine of the University of Lagos is involved in the training of hundreds of medical, dental, pharmacy and other allied health science students,” Bode said. Over the years, like many other things in Nigeria, LUTH has been abandoned by successive governments. Industry experts identified funding as being epileptic, amid increasing number of patients in a country where poverty is dealing a deadly blow on a huge percentage of the populace. While physical structures are still at the same place, maintenance has been a huge headache. LUTH grapples staff shortage, amid brain drain The facility has been grappling with shortage of personnel following the emigration of medical doctors from the country in the past years. item.title: Charting lasting path for Flamingos, other rising football stars
item.description: On Saturday, November 7, Nigeria’s Flamingos edged out Asian giants Japan 2-1 in Rabat, Morocco, to lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. They became the first African nation to claim the global title and placed Nigeria alongside France as the only countries to win both the men’s and women’s U-17 World Cups. The Flamingos’ male counterparts, the Golden Eaglets—with five titles—remain the most successful team in the world at that level. The victorious Flamingos returned to Nigeria on Monday, November 9, to a rousing welcome. Yet amid the national celebrations, federal cash rewards, and Senate commendations, a familiar anxiety lingers over the future of the young players. For decades, Nigeria has dominated youth tournaments, only to watch many of its brightest teenage sensations fade into obscurity. While stars like Victor Osimhen and Asisat Oshoala successfully transitioned to the global stage, countless others, hampered by poor management, unhealed injuries, or structural neglect, abandoned football altogether before their prime. Indeed, the history of Nigerian football is replete with stories of teenage sensations who sparkled at dawn with youth national teams only to fade into obscurity before noon. Thus, in spite of Nigeria’s dominance at the U-17 level, the country is yet to taste global victory at the U-20 level. The Flying Eagles, the team meant to harness the best talent from victorious U-17 squads, have managed to claim only two silver medals and one bronze since their first appearance in 1983. Similarly, only a handful of players have successfully transitioned from the U-17 to the U-20 and senior Super Eagles squads. Nduka Ugbade, Jonathan Akpoborie, Celestine Babayaro, Mikel Obi, Chinedu Obasi, Lukman Haruna, Ramon Azeez, Isaac Success and Taiwo Awoniyi are among the few who completed the full international pathway. Nigerias’ Flamingos U17 celebrating their World Cup win To ensure the 2026 Flamingos squad, and the next generation of young Nigerian athletes, don’t become cautionary tales, Nigerian football administrators must shift their focus from one-off tournament celebrations to sustainable career architecture. One of the biggest leaks in Nigerian football happens immediately after a youth tournament ends. Without a centralised database, young players return to disorganised local setups and vanish from national team radars. It is, therefore, a step in the right direction that the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has promised to preserve the core of the victorious Flamingos, with 11 players still eligible for the next U-17 competition. Meanwhile, the federation stated that others would be groomed for the U-20 national team, the Falconets, and eventually the Super Falcons. To achieve this objective, the NFF and the National Sports Commission (NSC) must maintain a strict digital registry for every youth international. Standout U-17 players should be systematically integrated into the U-20 Falconets and invited to understudy senior

item.title: Tunde Bakare: The Preacher, The Politician And Two Divorcees, by Emmanuel Aziken
item.description: Many years ago, Pastor Tunde Bakare’s voice was particularly outstanding in the debate over the misuse of anointing oil, especially olive oil, as an effigy of the power of God. Many of us, including your correspondent, then based in Kaduna, were particularly enchanted by his one-hour Sunday evening television broadcasts on Channels Television where he blended Old Testament religious proclamations with contemporary political discourse in a manner that was both captivating and intellectually engaging. He was in the mould of Elijah, who challenged the wicked King Ahab; John the Baptist, who confronted Herod; and Jesus Christ, who fearlessly challenged the religious establishment and the political order represented by the likes of Herod, whom He described as a fox. Bakare projected the image of a preacher who was not afraid to speak truth to power, whether in the church or in government. His interventions were often forceful, his biblical references uncompromising, and his denunciations of religious excesses particularly refreshing to many who believed that the pulpit should remain a place of truth and accountability. The questions about Bakare, however, began to emerge after he joined the political fray. His association with Muhammadu Buhari during the 2011 election cycle was his first major public adventure into partisan politics. The political partnership did not produce the expected electoral outcome. Some questioned his movement from the pulpit to the political podium, particularly against the backdrop of scriptural cautions about the tension between spiritual devotion and the worldly considerations that often drive political contests. His less-than-expected reaction to the killings of mostly Christian National Youth Service Corps members in the aftermath of the 2011 election would also have disappointed many who had looked up to him as a moral voice. Yet, his political journey continued. Before the 2023 presidential election, Bakare made an even more remarkable declaration: that he would become Nigeria’s 16th president. Many, including yours sincerely, took the pronouncement seriously, largely because of the regard in which he was held as a servant of God. A preacher who speaks with such certainty about the future, particularly when presenting it as a divine revelation, invites people to believe that his words are informed by something beyond personal ambition. The outcome of the APC presidential primary in June 2022 was therefore particularly instructive. Pastor Bakare scored zero votes. Since the emergence of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu as Nigeria’s 16th president, not much has been heard from Bakare in the kind of forceful public interventions that once defined his ministry. That is until recent reports about his role in, or apparent sanction of, the marriage of two previously married individuals: former actor and pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his new wife, Moya Jasmine Daniel, who was previously married to British-Nigerian gospel music producer Mo

item.title: Nigerians destroying Nigerians for money, by Muyiwa Adetiba
item.description: The harm Nigerian importers have done to the Chinese brand is incalculable. For years, we had been led to believe that Chinese products were inferior. Even now, despite empirical evidence to the contrary, I still hesitate to buy Chinese spare parts whether they are for my car or house. That is how deep the ‘brainwashing’ has gone. And it is not without reason. Several Chinese goods which were branded as cheaper had disappointed in the past. But the same Chinese goods were making in-roads into European and American markets with relative ease. These are countries that are historically fussy about standards for imported goods. How can a country that has become so industrialized that it is giving the almighty US sleepless nights be so negatively branded in Nigeria? The mystery was confounding. Yet the answer turned out to be relatively simple. Nigerian importers, AKA as ‘businessmen’ went and combed the hinterland in China to deliberately access or request for inferior goods, and sometimes scraps, for greater profit. In other words, Nigerians made Nigeria a dumping ground. And the regulating authorities were complicit to say the least because these goods pass through our borders and ports. This was the same thing they reportedly did with pharmaceutical products from India as that Asian country was emerging as the pharmaceutical capital of the world with its cheaper, generic versions of branded drugs. Things got so bad that many popular antibiotic brands had either been faked or their potency significantly reduced. The result was that drugs that were supposed to heal caused deaths. Inexplicable and sometimes painful deaths. Doctors started prescribing less common but probably more expensive alternatives just to protect the lives of their patients. Nothing I have stated here is unknown to the average Nigerian, let alone the relevant authorities. These fake goods and drugs must have come in shiploads to have made the kind of impact they had made. Yet, where are the authorities? Where is intelligence? Our official borders, with their several layers of government agents, are probably among the most manned in the world. They are adept at straining gnats while allowing camels a safe passage. Meanwhile, NAFDAC is fighting for needless turf with Nigerian Heart Foundation over certification of some drugs. Talk about leaving leprosy to fight scabies. Seems to me that authorities can be blind, deaf and dumb when there is no personal gratification in an assignment even if it is of dire national consequence. It gets worse. Fake products are no longer coming through our borders alone. Factories, of different sizes are being set up to ‘manufacture’ all manner of things. Many of the factories are not hidden. Many of the distributors know the products they are helping to push into the market are fake. Many of the pharmacies, supermarkets and retailers know the products they are selling to the public are sub-standard if not fake. Yet, every fake product that enters the

item.title: 2027: Aaro Meta urges Kwara South APC to back Danladi
item.description: By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin A political pressure group in Kwara South, Aaro Meta, has urged aggrieved members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the district to set aside their grievances and support the party’s governorship candidate, Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, Rt. Hon. Yakubu Salihu Danladi, ahead of the 2027 general elections. The group also backed the emergence of a governorship candidate from Kwara North, arguing that equity, fairness and political balance informed the need for a shift in power to the district. The group’s Coordinator, Engr. Adebayo S. Daramola, made the appeal on Friday while addressing journalists at the News Keg organised by the Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) in Ilorin. Aaro Meta said it played an active role in the 2018 O to Ge movement, which contributed to the emergence of the APC-led government in the state in 2019, adding that its position was informed by the need to sustain the party’s political fortunes and promote fairness among the three senatorial districts. The group recalled that during the 2019 governorship election, it supported the emergence of an APC candidate from Kwara Central, despite its base in Kwara South, in consideration of the prevailing political circumstances. That decision, it noted, resulted in the emergence of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who won the 2019 election and secured a second term in 2023. It urged APC members in Kwara South to demonstrate a similar spirit of political accommodation by supporting Danladi, who hails from Kwara North. “Why can’t we also have a free mind like we did in 2019 to rally support for any candidate that emerged from the Kwara North Senatorial District, rather than having a preferred candidate?” the group queried. Aaro Meta acknowledged that Kwara South had aspired to produce the APC governorship candidate but maintained that political power should be distributed fairly among the three senatorial districts. It argued that since 1999, Kwara South had produced a governor for eight years, while Kwara Central would have accounted for 20 years in office by the time AbdulRazaq completes his tenure in May 2027. item.title: Emefiele: Court admits Supreme Court judgment in forfeiture case
item.description: —Restricts use of document in ongoing criminal trial By Henry Ojelu The Lagos State Special Offences Court, Ikeja, on Friday admitted a Supreme Court judgment tendered by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, in the ongoing trial of former Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, Godwin Emefiele, over the forfeiture of properties allegedly linked to him. However, the trial judge, Justice Rahman Oshodi, ruled that although the judgment was admissible, it could not be used for or against any of the parties in the criminal proceedings. Ruling on objections raised by the defence, led by Olalekan Ojo, SAN, and submissions by the prosecution, led by the Federal Director of Public Prosecutions, Rotimi Oyedepo, SAN, Justice Oshodi held that the document was a public document and a certified true copy of a Supreme Court decision. The judge consequently admitted it as Exhibit A but restricted its use in the trial. He said: “The judgment is a public document, and it is a certified true copy of the Supreme Court decision. It would be accepted as an exhibit (in rem), but cannot be used in the case either for or against any party.” Justice Oshodi explained that the document satisfied the legal requirements for admissibility under the Evidence Act. On the defence’s objection that the prosecution tendered only the lead judgment without the separate judgments of other Supreme Court justices, the judge relied on the Court of Appeal decision in Matthias Sikiri and Others v. Nketchukwu Onyema and Others (2021) LPELR-56552(CA). He also cited Avacha and Others v. Fawole, where the Supreme Court held that the lead judgment represents the decision of the court. Addressing concerns over the use of a judgment arising from civil forfeiture proceedings in a criminal trial, Justice Oshodi said the restriction on its use had adequately addressed the issue. Citing David Itauma v. Friday Jasi, the judge said previous judgments tendered in subsequent proceedings were intended to establish what was decided in the earlier cases and not to prove the guilt or innocence of parties in the subsequent proceedings. He consequently overruled the defence objection and admitted the document. Earlier, Ojo had opposed its admission, arguing that the judgment was irrelevant to the charges against his client, incomplete without the other justices’ opinions and arose from non-conviction-based civil forfeiture proceedings. Counsel to the second defendant, A.M. Kotoye, SAN, aligned himself with the objection and urged the court to reject the document. However, Oyedepo argued that the judgment was admissible as a certified true copy of a Supreme Court decision, adding that the prosecution had complied with Sections 103 and 104 of the Evidence Act. He maintained that the fact that only the lead judgment was tendered did not affect its admissibility, while the civil nature of the forfeiture proceedings did not make the document inadmissible. item.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
item.description: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. item.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Future/Josh Dinner, Space.com) Ship goes to orbit Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to plan after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment." Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28. Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch. The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which currently number more than 11,000 in LEO. The addition of this new set of V3s will add a terabit of data capacity to the constellation, according to SpaceX's Flight 15 mission outline . That's equivalent to the

item.title: FAA lifts ground stop after hours-long delays snag travelers
item.description: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop. Original story below: "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related. We'll update this story as more information becomes available.® Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. Updated to add at 2353 UTC CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment. item.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
item.description: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

item.title: Who Gets To Compete?
item.description: Opposition talks are continuing. Campaigns are gathering pace. But access, legal certainty and confidence in the vote are becoming defining questions of the election. In Yelwata, Peter Obi stood before a community carrying the wounds of mass violence. In Akure, the APC called its organisation to work for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election. In London, INEC’s chairman faced questions about whether Nigerians could trust the coming vote. These were different settings for the same election. Together, they reveal a contest in which persuading voters is only part of the task. Candidates must sustain their organisations, establish their right to participate and reach citizens safely. The electoral commission must demonstrate that those citizens’ choices will be recorded faithfully. The week’s developments sharpen a fundamental question: how open, credible and competitive will the road to 2027 remain? Lagos Raises the Stakes Thursday’s reported attack on an NDC town hall gathering in Oregun, Lagos, deserves particular attention. According to reporting from the scene, armed men disrupted the gathering, participants were injured and a suspect was arrested. The NDC alleged political responsibility; the Lagos APC denied sponsoring the incident. The report established no independent evidence linking the attackers to a political party. Investigation must establish who acted, who organised them and whether anyone provided support. The democratic principle requires no such delay: citizens must be able to attend lawful political meetings without fearing assault. Violence can influence an election before a ballot is cast. It can discourage attendance, make venues reluctant to host meetings, increase campaign costs and persuade volunteers to stay home. Its effects therefore extend beyond the immediate victims. When intimidation restricts participation, it changes the conditions under which candidates compete. Political leaders should condemn attacks consistently, including when the victims support their opponents. Security agencies must provide protection on the same basis. Makinde Keeps the Alliance Door Open Seyi Makinde’s latest comments give fresh substance to the opposition’s continuing conversation about cooperation. In an interview reported today, the Oyo governor confirmed active discussions involving Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi. He said decisions should draw on evidence, manifestos, previous performance and public sentiment. He did not announce an agreement or endorse a preferred candidate. That distinction separates a development worth watching from a coalition already formed. The negotiations face a familiar practical difficulty: cooperation requires choices that impose costs on participants. Someone may need to surrender an ambition, accept another candidate’s leadership or persuade supporters to work with former rivals. An agreement also needs to travel beyond the negotiating room.
